dimension_description: Length measures the distance between two points, yet it spans everything from the Planck length, where spacetime ripples like quantum foam, to the 93-billion-light-year reach of the observable universe. Across these 61 orders of magnitude, the same physical laws shape quarks, atoms, planets, and galaxies. If the universe were the size of Earth, a human would be smaller than an atom.

items.description: A length constructed from the constants of quantum mechanics, gravity, and relativity. It marks the scale at which we expect our separate descriptions of these forces to need a quantum theory of gravity. Ideas such as spacetime foam and black-hole limits on measurement make it a compelling frontier, but it has not been established experimentally as the smallest possible distance. The ruler shows a derived scale, not an observed grain of spacetime.

items.description: The weak force, which lets the Sun fuse hydrogen and makes some atomic nuclei decay, reaches only about 2.5 billionths of a billionth of a meter. Its carriers, the W and Z bosons, are about 86 times heavier than a proton, and a force carried by heavy particles fades within roughly their reduced Compton wavelength, here hbar divided by the W mass times the speed of light. A proton is about 340 times wider than the reach of this force.

items.description: The classical electron radius, an electromagnetic length scale derived from its charge and rest energy, not an observed electron size. Electrons appear point-like in experiments. In the classical picture, spreading a charge over a small sphere stores electrostatic energy; equating a characteristic Coulomb energy to the electron's rest energy gives this scale. The exact self-energy depends on the assumed charge distribution, so it does not define a physical surface for the electron.

items.description: Replace hydrogen's electron with a muon, its 207-times-heavier cousin, and the atom shrinks about 186 times, to roughly 0.57 picometers across. The muon then orbits only about 340 proton radii out, close enough that its energy levels reveal the proton's size. Measurements of muonic hydrogen in 2010 found a proton smaller than electron-based experiments did, a puzzle that later work largely resolved in favor of the smaller value. A muon decays in about two microseconds.

This is a wavelength, not the particle's physical size; increasing its energy makes the wavelength shorter. Trillions of neutrinos pass through your body every second from the Sun, and most pass through the Earth without interacting. Their tiny mass and ghostly nature make them crucial messengers from stellar cores and supernova explosions.

items.description: A hydrogen atom is about 106 picometers across if its edge is drawn at the Bohr radius, 52.9 pm, the electron's most probable distance from the proton. The electron has no orbit or surface; it is a probability cloud, and only about 32% of it lies inside that sphere, thinning out exponentially beyond. The proton at the center is roughly 60,000 times smaller than the sphere, so the atom is almost entirely empty space. This marker is the diameter of the Bohr-radius sphere.

items.description:
The 140 pm marker is twice carbon's **empirical atomic radius** of 70 pm, a useful comparison number rather than an edge you could touch. Carbon's nonbonded, van der Waals radius is about 170 pm, so the two conventions answer different questions.

In the explorer, dots sample where carbon's six electrons are likely to be and stop at the 70 pm sphere, which holds a little over half of their probability. The tight blue core is the 1s pair; the amber cloud is the 2s pair; and the green and rose dumbbells are the two occupied 2p orbitals, which point at right angles to each other and give carbon its directional bonds. The orbitals are hydrogen-like approximations with screened nuclear charges, not an exact six-electron solution. [WebElements lists both radii](https://webelements.co.uk/carbon/atom_sizes.html).

items.description: Water's bend matters more than its rough diameter. Its two O–H bonds meet at about 104.5°, so their electrical polarities reinforce rather than cancel; neighboring molecules can then form a shifting network of hydrogen bonds. In an isolated molecule, each O–H distance is only 0.958 Å, as recorded in [NIST's experimental geometry](https://cccbdb.nist.gov/expgeom2x.asp?casno=7732185).

Remarkably, proteins can fold from random coils to precise shapes in microseconds.

items.description: SARS-CoV-2, the coronavirus behind COVID-19, is a roughly spherical particle about 91 nm across. Its fatty envelope is studded with a few dozen spike proteins that reach another 20 nm or so outward and latch onto ACE2 receptors on human cells. Inside, a single strand of RNA about 30,000 letters long is one of the largest genomes of any RNA virus. This marker is the mean envelope diameter measured by cryo-electron tomography, not counting the spikes; viruses as a group range from about 20 nm to more than a micrometer.

items.description: From the ground at its star-shaped fort to the tip of the torch, the Statue of Liberty stands 93 m (305 ft) tall. Half of that is the copper statue itself, 46 m from base to torch; the rest is Richard Morris Hunt's granite pedestal and the walls of Fort Wood beneath it. The trench is deeper than Mount Everest is tall, and only three people have ever reached its bottom.

Light takes 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel this distance, meaning we see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago. This distance varies by 5 million km due to Earth's elliptical orbit, affecting our seasons and climate.
items.name: Astronomical Unit
items.summary_short: The distance from Earth to the Sun, known as one astronomical unit - the yardstick of the solar system.

items.description: Jupiter orbits the Sun at an average distance of 778 million km, about 5.2 times Earth's distance, so sunlight takes roughly 43 minutes to reach it and the planet needs almost 12 years to circle the Sun once. Its orbit lies just outside the asteroid belt, and the planet is heavier than all the other planets combined, more than twice over. The orbit would be swallowed whole by the largest red supergiants.

items.description: The diameter of Betelgeuse, a red supergiant star that could explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years. This massive star is so large that if placed at the center of our solar system, it would extend beyond Jupiter's orbit. Betelgeuse is one of the brightest stars in the night sky and appears red due to its cool surface temperature. When it explodes, it will be visible during daylight and brighter than the full Moon.

items.description: Alpha Centauri A and B, a Sun-like star and a slightly smaller orange one, circle each other along an ellipse about 47 AU long, once every 79.8 years. They approach to 11.2 AU, about the distance from the Sun to Saturn, and recede to 35.6 AU, about the distance from the Sun to Pluto. The pair belongs to the nearest star system to the Sun, together with the faint red dwarf Proxima Centauri.

items.description: The Kuiper Belt is a wide ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, stretching from about 30 AU to roughly 50 AU from the Sun, so about 100 AU across counting both sides. It is 20 times as wide as the asteroid belt and 20 to 200 times as massive, yet its total mass is only about 2 percent of Earth's. Pluto lives here, and its main population ends abruptly near 48 AU for reasons still debated.

Only two spacecraft, Voyager 1 and 2, have ever left this protective bubble.

items.description: A representative 200,000-au diameter of the hypothesized Oort Cloud, using the upper end of NASA's uncertain 10,000-100,000-au outer-radius range. This vast reservoir of icy objects lies at the outer reaches of our solar system rather than having a directly observed sharp edge. This distant region contains trillions of comets and extends halfway to the nearest star. The Oort Cloud is the source of long-period comets that occasionally visit the inner solar system. These icy bodies are pristine remnants from the solar system's formation, preserving the original composition of the protoplanetary disk.

This red dwarf star is part of the Alpha Centauri triple star system and is 4.24 light-years away. At current spacecraft speeds, it would take 75,000 years to reach Proxima Centauri. items.description: The Pillars of Creation rise about five light-years within the Eagle Nebula, columns of cold hydrogen gas mixed with dust. Ultraviolet light from nearby massive stars heats and erodes their exposed surfaces, while denser material shelters gas beneath it and stars form deep inside. Their height exceeds the distance from the Sun to Proxima Centauri, turning a familiar astronomical photograph into a structure on an interstellar scale.

About 6,500 light-years from Earth, its filaments are still expanding at roughly 1,500 km/s and are now about 11 light-years across. At its center, a pulsar spinning about 30 times per second powers the whole nebula's glow.

items.description: The size of the Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery visible to the naked eye where hundreds of new stars are being born. This massive cloud of gas and dust contains enough material to form 2,000 Sun-like stars. The nebula glows because young, hot stars ionize the surrounding hydrogen gas. It's one of the most studied objects in astronomy and provides insights into how solar systems like ours form from collapsing clouds.

items.description: The Pleiades is an open star cluster about 444 light-years away with more than 1,000 members, of which the naked eye picks out only the brightest handful as the Seven Sisters. Its core has a radius of about 8 light-years, but the cluster's gravity binds stars out to a tidal radius of about 43 light-years, so the whole cluster is roughly 86 light-years across. It is young, and its stars will slowly drift apart over time.

It is so massive and complex, with several distinct generations of stars, that astronomers suspect it is the stripped core of a small galaxy swallowed long ago by the Milky Way. To the naked eye it looks like a single fuzzy star.

The Milky Way is on a collision course with the Andromeda Galaxy, which will merge with us in 4.5 billion years.

units.description: The fundamental unit of length, defined as the distance light travels in vacuum during 1/299,792,458 seconds. This definition makes the meter a universal constant based on the speed of light, ensuring precision across all scientific measurements. The meter serves as the reference for all other length units and forms the foundation for dimensional analysis in physics and engineering. Remarkably, this definition means the speed of light is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second by definition.
units.name: meters

units.description: A unit of length in the imperial system, originally based on the length of a human foot. This practical unit is defined as exactly 0.3048 meters through international agreement. The foot is widely used in construction, aviation, and maritime applications, particularly in the United States. Interestingly, the foot was standardized in 1959 when the international yard was redefined, making it exactly 12 inches. This unit provides a convenient scale for human-scale measurements and remains deeply embedded in American culture.
units.name: feet

units.description: A unit of length in the imperial system, defined as exactly 25.4 millimeters through international standardization. The inch provides high precision for measurements requiring fine resolution, particularly in manufacturing, engineering, and scientific applications. This unit is derived from the width of a human thumb and has been standardized across different measurement systems. The inch serves as a fundamental building block for larger imperial units and enables precise dimensional specifications. Interestingly, the inch was redefined in 1959 to be exactly 2.54 centimeters, creating a precise metric conversion.
units.name: inches

units.description: A metric unit of length equal to 1,000 meters, representing the most commonly used unit for terrestrial distances. The kilometer provides an optimal scale for measuring distances on Earth, from city blocks to continental spans. This unit is fundamental to transportation, geography, and Earth sciences, enabling precise navigation and spatial analysis. The kilometer serves as the standard unit for expressing distances in most countries worldwide. Interestingly, the kilometer was originally defined as 1/10,000 of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator through Paris.
units.name: kilometers

units.description: A unit of length in the imperial system, defined as exactly 1,609.344 meters through international standardization. The mile represents a practical unit for measuring longer distances, particularly in transportation and navigation applications. This unit is derived from the Roman 'mille passus' (thousand paces) and has evolved into a standard measure for road distances, speed limits, and athletic competitions. The mile remains deeply embedded in American culture, with phrases like 'miles per hour' and 'miles per gallon' being everyday expressions. Interestingly, the nautical mile is different, being based on one minute of latitude.
units.name: miles

units.description: A unit of astronomical distance representing the distance traveled by light in vacuum during one Julian year (365.25 days). The light-year provides a natural scale for measuring interstellar and intergalactic distances, where conventional units become impractical. This unit is fundamental to astronomy and cosmology, enabling precise measurements of stellar distances, galactic dimensions, and cosmic expansion. The light-year represents both a distance and a time measurement, reflecting the finite speed of light in the universe. Interestingly, when we look at stars, we're seeing them as they were years or even millennia ago due to light travel time.
